passage:
The fair was crowded and loud. Manoj, running with his balloon, bumped into Jaya and her ice cream fell in the dust. Jaya's face crumpled. Manoj had only one coin left, not enough for another ice cream. He stared at it, then at her. "Sorry, Jaya. I didn't look." He held out his half-eaten candy floss. "You can have the rest."
Jaya sniffed and took a pink handful. "Next time, look," she said, and they walked on together.

qa.q: What fell in the dust?
qa.a: Jaya's ice cream fell in the dust.

qa.q: What does Manoj staring at his coin and then at Jaya suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was worried and wanted to fix what he'd done, even though he couldn't buy a new ice cream.

qa.q: How did Manoj make amends?
qa.a: He said sorry and offered his candy floss, sharing what he had.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel about Manoj's offer?
qa.a: She might still be a bit upset but feel better that he cared enough to share.

grounding: It shows a child repairing harm by apologising and sharing what he has despite a constraint.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Lokesh grabbed Deepak's toy car, swung it too hard and snapped off a wheel. Deepak shouted, "You broke it!" Lokesh hid behind the curtain. After a while he came out holding the wheel. "Sorry, Dada. Can we fix it?" They sat at the table with glue and tape. Lokesh held the car very still while Deepak fixed the wheel. When it rolled again, Lokesh smiled shyly.

qa.q: What did Lokesh snap off Deepak's toy car?
qa.a: He snapped off a wheel.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh hide behind the curtain?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and scared of Deepak's anger after breaking the car.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that helped repair the harm?
qa.a: He said sorry, brought the wheel back and helped hold the car still while it was fixed.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel after they fix the car together?
qa.a: He might feel less angry and more willing to forgive because Lokesh helped.

grounding: It shows a child apologising and helping to repair a broken toy.

passage:
"Vijay, where's Saurabh's pencil box?"
"I don't know."
"The blue one with rockets? Hmm."
Vijay looked at his feet. Then he opened his bag. "It's here. I liked it."
"What can you do now?"
Vijay walked to Saurabh. "Sorry. I took it. Here." He held it out with both hands.
Saurabh took it and checked the rockets. "You can use the rocket pencil tomorrow," he said.

qa.q: What was on Saurabh's pencil box?
qa.a: It had rockets on it.

qa.q: What does Vijay looking at his feet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt guilty about taking the pencil box.

qa.q: What could the adult say to Vijay after he returned it?
qa.a: They could thank him for returning it and saying sorry, and suggest asking first next time.

qa.q: How does Saurabh react to Vijay's apology?
qa.a: He accepts it and even offers to let Vijay use the rocket pencil tomorrow.

grounding: It shows a child repairing harm by admitting, saying sorry and returning an item.

passage:
Note from Seema, kindergarten teacher, Friday:

During art, Gopika, five, grabbed her friend's crayon and tore her friend's drawing by accident. Her friend cried. Gopika stood still for a moment, then said, "Sorry, I didn't mean it." She fetched tape and helped stick the drawing back, then gave back the crayon.

What I did next: I thanked Gopika for fixing it and asked her friend if she felt better. She nodded, and they finished drawing side by side.

qa.q: What did Gopika fetch after tearing the drawing?
qa.a: She fetched tape and helped stick the drawing back.

qa.q: What does Gopika standing still for a moment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt shocked and sorry when she saw her friend cry.

qa.q: How did Seema support Gopika's repair?
qa.a: Seema thanked Gopika for fixing the drawing and checked on her friend, showing that making amends matters to both children.

qa.q: How might Gopika's friend feel after the repair?
qa.a: She seemed to feel better and comforted, since they went back to drawing side by side.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child apologising, helping repair and returning an item.

passage:
Near the village well, Vaibhav, six, had a secret: Ojas's green marble, the shiny one, hidden in his pocket. He'd picked it up when Ojas wasn't looking.

All day it felt heavy. At dinner he couldn't finish his roti.

In the evening he ran to Ojas's house. "I took your marble," he said, holding it out. "Sorry."

Ojas stared, then grabbed it. "You took it?"

"I'm sorry. You can have my red one too."

Ojas thought. Then he smiled. "Let's play tomorrow."

qa.q: What colour was the marble Vaibhav took?
qa.a: It was Ojas's green marble, the shiny one.

qa.q: How can you tell Vaibhav felt guilty about the marble?
qa.a: The marble "felt heavy" all day and he couldn't finish his roti, which shows it was weighing on him.

qa.q: What made Vaibhav's apology strong?
qa.a: He returned the marble, said sorry clearly and offered his red one too, repairing the harm rather than only saying words.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when Vaibhav admitted it?
qa.a: He was surprised and maybe a bit upset at first, then forgave him and wanted to play again.

grounding: Shows a young child in a village making amends by returning a taken item and apologising.

passage:
In the kindergarten in Helsinki, Paulo, five, ran past the block corner and knocked down Sami's tall tower.
Sami's face crumpled. “My tower!”
Paulo stopped. He looked at the blocks on the floor and at Sami's tears.
“Sorry,” he said. “It was an accident.”
Sami still cried.
Paulo knelt down. “I'll help build it again. Bigger.”
He handed Sami a red block. Sami sniffed and took it. Soon the tower was taller than before.

qa.q: What did Paulo knock down?
qa.a: He knocked down Sami's tall tower.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel when he saw Sami crying?
qa.a: He felt sorry and a bit guilty, so he stopped and apologised.

qa.q: What did Paulo do besides saying sorry, and why did it help?
qa.a: He helped rebuild the tower, which showed he really wanted to fix the harm.

qa.q: How did Sami feel when Paulo handed him a block?
qa.a: He began to feel better and less upset, accepting Paulo's help.

grounding: A five-year-old repairs an accident by apologising and helping rebuild.

passage:
In the school library, Divyansh, five, was turning pages too fast. Rrrip. A page of the elephant book tore halfway.
He looked around. Nobody had seen. He could put it back on the shelf.
Instead he carried it to the desk. “Ma'am, I tore it. Sorry.”
Ms Parul looked at the page, then at him. “Thank you for telling me. Shall we fix it?”
She gave him the tape. Divyansh stuck it very carefully, tongue between his teeth.

qa.q: Which book did Divyansh tear?
qa.a: He tore a page of the elephant book.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel when he tore the page?
qa.a: He felt worried and guilty, looking around to see if anyone had seen.

qa.q: How did Ms Parul help Divyansh make amends?
qa.a: She thanked him for telling and let him fix the page with tape himself.

qa.q: How might Ms Parul feel about Divyansh's honesty?
qa.a: She likely feels pleased and proud that he told the truth instead of hiding it.

grounding: A five-year-old admits tearing a library book and helps repair it.

passage:
I'm Aditi, Tarun's big sister. On Sunday I saw him come home from the neighbour's with Chintu's toy car in his pocket.
At dinner he was very quiet. He kept touching his pocket.
After dinner he got his crayons and drew a car with a big heart. He wrote a wobbly “SORY.”
Then he asked me to walk with him next door. He gave Chintu the car and the drawing. “I took it. Sorry.”
Chintu grinned and let him play with it for five minutes.

qa.q: What did Tarun draw?
qa.a: He drew a car with a big heart.

qa.q: Why was Tarun quiet at dinner?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and uneasy about taking Chintu's car.

qa.q: What was good about how Tarun made amends?
qa.a: He returned the car, said sorry and gave a drawing, repairing the harm in more than one way.

qa.q: How did Chintu react to Tarun's apology?
qa.a: Chintu was happy and forgiving, grinning and sharing the car with Tarun.

grounding: An older sister observes her little brother return a taken toy and apologise.

passage:
On Monday, Dilnaz knocked Mridul's clay pot off the windowsill. It cracked in two. She pushed the pieces behind the curtain and ran outside.
On Tuesday, Mridul searched everywhere, looking sad. Dilnaz watched from the door, chewing her sleeve. Then she pulled back the curtain. "I broke it. Sorry."
Mridul's eyes filled up. "It was for Ammi."
On Thursday, Dilnaz sat with Mridul and helped him roll new clay. She pressed a flower into the side. "Now it's from both of us."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz push the pieces of the pot?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: Why was Dilnaz chewing her sleeve on Tuesday?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt guilty and nervous, watching Mridul search for the pot she had hidden.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do to make amends, beyond saying sorry?
qa.a: She helped Mridul make a new pot and added a flower, which repaired some of the harm.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel on Thursday compared with Tuesday?
qa.a: On Tuesday Mridul was sad and hurt; by Thursday he probably feels comforted that Dilnaz helped make something new for Ammi.

grounding: Over a few days a child owns up to breaking a pot and helps make a new one.

passage:
The monsoon drain by the school gate was rushing. Hemant set his paper boat on the water, and Eshaan, running past, knocked it under. It was gone.
Hemant burst into tears. The bus would leave in five minutes.
Eshaan stood in the rain, not moving. Then he tore a page from his own notebook. "Sorry. I'll make you one."
His fingers were wet and slow. The bus honked. He folded fast, crooked, and held it out.
Hemant sniffed and took it. "It's wonky."
"Sorry," Eshaan said again. "It still floats."

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the bus would leave?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he stood in the rain, not moving?
qa.a: Eshaan felt guilty and unsure what to do after seeing Hemant cry.

qa.q: How did Eshaan make amends under time pressure?
qa.a: He said sorry and quickly made a new boat from his own notebook, giving something back for what he broke.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemant to get the wonky boat?
qa.a: Hemant is still a little sad, but he feels Eshaan cares and has tried to fix it.

grounding: In the monsoon rain a child apologises and makes a replacement boat before the bus leaves.

passage:
At the Lohri bonfire in the colony, Madhav grabbed Eshaan's packet of rewri and ran off laughing. When he came back, the packet was half empty.
Eshaan's face fell. "That was mine."
Madhav held the packet behind his back. He looked at the fire, then at Eshaan.
"Sorry," he said, and handed it over. "I ate some."
Eshaan still looked upset.
Madhav went to his mother and asked for his own packet. He poured half into Eshaan's. "Now it's full again."
Eshaan smiled and tossed a few into the fire.

qa.q: What did Madhav grab from Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan's packet of rewri.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he looked at the fire, then at Eshaan?
qa.a: Madhav felt guilty and unsure, realising the joke had upset Eshaan.

qa.q: Why did Madhav's second step matter after saying sorry?
qa.a: Eshaan was still upset, so replacing the rewri from his own packet repaired the harm, not just the words.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Madhav's apology?
qa.a: Eshaan feels his loss was taken seriously and is glad his packet is full again 😊.

grounding: At a winter Lohri bonfire, a child returns a snack and makes up what he ate.

passage:
"You broke my kite!" Nitin shouted on the Sankranti terrace.
Siddharth, five, looked at the torn paper. "I didn't mean to."
"But you did!"
Siddharth's lip wobbled. Their grandfather said, "What can you do now?"
Siddharth thought. "Say sorry?"
"And?"
"Fix it?"
He found tape and held the paper while Grandpa stuck it. "Sorry, Nitin."
Nitin sniffed. "Okay. You can fly it with me."

qa.q: What did Siddharth break?
qa.a: Nitin's kite.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when Nitin shouted?
qa.a: He felt upset and guilty; his lip wobbled.

qa.q: What helped Siddharth make amends?
qa.a: Grandpa's question helped him think of saying sorry and fixing the kite.

qa.q: How does Nitin feel after the kite is fixed?
qa.a: Nitin feels calmer and forgiving, inviting Siddharth to fly it with him.

grounding: Shows a young child repairing harm by apologising and helping fix a broken toy.

passage:
Kindergarten note, winter term
During sand play, Francis (5) threw sand at Asif, which got in his eyes. Asif cried.
Francis froze. I asked him to see how Asif was feeling. He said, "Sad." Then he went to Asif and said, "Sorry. I'll get you water." He brought a cup of water and sat beside him.
Asif calmed down. They built a sand road together after. I've shared this with both families.

qa.q: What did Francis bring Asif?
qa.a: A cup of water.

qa.q: How did Francis seem to feel after the sand hit Asif?
qa.a: He seemed shocked and sorry, freezing before he went to help.

qa.q: How did the teacher guide Francis to make amends?
qa.a: The teacher asked him to notice Asif's feelings, which led Francis to say sorry and help.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Francis brings water?
qa.a: Asif likely feels comforted and willing to play again.

grounding: A teacher records a young child apologising and helping after hurting a friend.

passage:
On the first day of the harvest fair in their village, Hemant, six, grabbed Jatin's balloon and it floated away.
Jatin cried.
Hemant stood there, hot-faced. Then he took the coin his mother had given him for sugarcane juice. He walked to the balloon seller and bought a new one.
"Sorry," he said, holding it out.
Jatin wiped his nose and took it. "Thanks."

qa.q: What did Hemant buy with his coin?
qa.a: A new balloon.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel after the balloon floated away?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and sorry, standing hot-faced.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Buying a new balloon and saying sorry, because it repaired the loss, not just the words.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel about the new balloon?
qa.a: Jatin probably feels better and ready to forgive.

grounding: Shows a young child making amends by replacing what he caused to be lost.

passage:
On a cold June morning at the Johannesburg preschool, Beatriz, five, snatched Thabo's woolly hat to tease him. It fell into a muddy puddle. Thabo's eyes filled with tears.
Beatriz stood still, her face hot. Then she fished the hat out and tried to wipe it on her jersey.
"I'm sorry, Thabo. I made it dirty."
Thabo sniffed. "It's my gogo's hat."
Beatriz pulled off her own scarf and wrapped it round his ears. "You can wear mine till it's dry."
Her twin brother Nuno watched, then brought paper towels from the bathroom.

qa.q: Whose hat was it, according to Thabo?
qa.a: It was his gogo's hat.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling when she stood still with a hot face?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sorry, seeing that her teasing had made Thabo cry.

qa.q: What made Beatriz's apology more than just words?
qa.a: She fished out the hat, tried to clean it, said sorry and lent her own scarf, so she helped repair the harm.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel with Beatriz's scarf round his ears?
qa.a: Thabo probably feels comforted and less upset, since she noticed his hurt and tried to make it better. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young child repairing harm by saying sorry, trying to fix the item and helping the child she hurt.
